sections.heading: Eight Classes of Pronouns
sections.rule: Pronouns may be divided into eight classes: Personal (including Possessive), Demonstrative, Relative, Interrogative, Distributive, Reflexive and Emphasising, Indefinite, and Reciprocal.
sections.bn: Pronoun-কে আটটি শ্রেণিতে ভাগ করা যায়: Personal, Demonstrative, Relative, Interrogative, Distributive, Reflexive & Emphasising, Indefinite এবং Reciprocal।
examples: Personal: I, you, he, she, it, we, they, mine, yours…
Demonstrative: this, that, these, those, such, so
Relative: who, which, that, what, as, whoever…
Interrogative: who, which, what…
Distributive: each, either, neither
Reflexive/Emphatic: myself, yourself, himself…
Indefinite: one, any, some, they…
Reciprocal: each other, one another

sections.heading: Three Persons
sections.rule: Personal Pronouns stand for persons. First Person = the speaker (I, we). Second Person = the person spoken to (you, thou). Third Person = the person spoken of (he, she, it, they).
sections.bn: Personal Pronoun ব্যক্তির পরিবর্তে ব্যবহৃত হয়। First Person = বক্তা (I, we)। Second Person = যাকে বলা হচ্ছে (you, thou)। Third Person = যার সম্পর্কে বলা হচ্ছে (he, she, it, they)।
examples: I am reading. (First Person)
You are listening. (Second Person)
He / She / They are coming. (Third Person)

sections.heading: Nominative, Possessive, Objective
sections.rule: Personal Pronouns change form according to case: Nominative (subject), Possessive (ownership), Objective (object of verb/preposition).
sections.bn: Personal Pronoun case অনুযায়ী রূপ বদলায়: Nominative (কর্তা), Possessive (অধিকার), Objective (কর্ম)।
examples: He knows. / I know the boy. (Nominative)
I saw her. / He talked with me. (Objective)

lessons.title: Correct Use of Subject & Object Forms

sections.heading: After verb to be
sections.rule: In formal English, after the verb to be use the nominative: It is I / Was it he? In informal conversation the objective is common: It's me / It was him.
sections.bn: Formal English-এ to be-এর পরে Nominative হয়: It is I। Informal-এ Objective চলে: It's me।
examples: Formal: It is I who helped you.
Informal: It's me.
It was he (not him) who arranged the meeting.
sections.caution: When the pronoun is subject of a following clause, always use nominative.

sections.heading: After between, but, let
sections.rule: Between is a preposition and takes objective case. But (preposition) takes objective. Let takes objective.
sections.bn: Between, but (preposition), let-এর পরে সবসময় Objective case হয়।
examples: Between you and me (not I).
Nobody was present but me (not I).
Let him and me do the job.

sections.heading: Possessive Adjectives vs Pronouns
sections.rule: My, thy, her, its, our, your, their are Possessive Adjectives (used before nouns). Mine, thine, hers, ours, yours, theirs are Possessive Pronouns (stand alone).
sections.bn: My, your, their ইত্যাদি noun-এর আগে বসে → Possessive Adjective। Mine, yours, theirs একা বসে → Possessive Pronoun।
examples: This is my book. (Adjective)
This book is mine. (Pronoun)
sections.caution: Never write her's, it's, your's, their's. Its (possessive) is not it's (it is).

sections.heading: Agreement of Gender & Number
sections.rule: The pronoun must match the gender and number of the noun it replaces. When sex is uncertain we often use it (especially for babies).
sections.bn: Pronoun-এর number ও gender noun-এর সাথে মিলতে হবে। লিঙ্গ অনিশ্চিত হলে সাধারণত it ব্যবহার হয়।
examples: The boy has done his work.
It is a healthy baby.

sections.heading: Thou, You, Ye
sections.rule: Thou is now rare except in poetry and prayer. You is used for both singular and plural and always takes a plural verb. Ye is an old form, mainly poetic.
sections.bn: Thou এখন প্রধানত কবিতা ও প্রার্থনায়। You একবচন ও বহুবচন উভয়েই ব্যবহৃত হয় এবং সবসময় plural verb নেয়।
examples: Thou art, O God!
Ram, you are a wise man.
Boys, you are to do this.

sections.heading: Many uses of It
sections.rule: It is used for animals (when sex not specified), babies, as preparatory subject, for inanimate objects, to emphasise, impersonally (It rains), for time/weather/distance.
sections.bn: It ব্যবহার হয়: পশু, শিশু, preparatory subject, বস্তু, জোর দেওয়ার জন্য, impersonal (It rains), সময়/আবহাওয়া।
examples: The dog follows its master.
It is good to swim.
It rains. / It is 5 o'clock.

sections.heading: This, That, These, Those, Such, So, One
sections.rule: When used alone they are Demonstrative Pronouns; with nouns they become adjectives. This/these = near; that/those = distant. When two nouns are mentioned, this = latter, that = former.
sections.bn: একা থাকলে Demonstrative Pronoun; noun-এর সাথে থাকলে Adjective। This/these = কাছের; that/those = দূরের।
examples: This is my house. That is yours.
Work and play are both necessary; this (=play) gives rest, that (=work) gives energy.

sections.heading: Who, Which, That, What
sections.rule: A Relative Pronoun joins sentences and refers to an Antecedent. Who → persons. Which → things, animals, babies. That → persons, animals, things. What → things (often = that which).
sections.bn: Relative Pronoun দুটি বাক্য যোগ করে এবং Antecedent-এর দিকে ইঙ্গিত করে। Who = ব্যক্তি। Which = বস্তু/পশু। That = সব। What = that which।
examples: I know the man who came.
This is the book which he bought.
I know what you say.

sections.heading: Nominative Who / Objective Whom
sections.rule: Who is nominative; whom is objective. In formal English use whom after prepositions and as object. In everyday speech who is often used for both.
sections.bn: Who = Nominative; Whom = Objective। Formal-এ preposition-এর পরে whom। Informal-এ who-ই চলে।
examples: The man who came was my uncle.
He is a person whom you can trust.
Who do you want to talk to? (informal)

sections.heading: Restrictive and Continuative
sections.rule: Restrictive: defines the antecedent (usually no comma). Continuative: adds extra information (usually with comma). That is always restrictive.
sections.bn: Restrictive = সীমাবদ্ধ করে। Continuative = অতিরিক্ত তথ্য দেয়। That সবসময় restrictive।
examples: This is the boy who did it. (Restrictive)
I saw your father, who recognised me. (Continuative)

sections.heading: As and But
sections.rule: As is a relative after same, such, as much, as many. But as relative means that not / who not (Negative Relative) after a negative word.
sections.bn: Same, such-এর পরে as relative হয়। But = যে না / who not (negative relative)।
examples: This is the same book as that.
There is no man but wishes to be happy.

sections.heading: Agreement and Omission
sections.rule: Relative pronouns agree in number, gender and person with their antecedents. The relative is often omitted when it is the object of a verb or preposition.
sections.bn: Relative তার antecedent-এর number, gender, person মেনে চলে। Object হলে relative প্রায়ই বাদ যায়।
examples: I who am your master say so.
He is the man (whom) I saw.

sections.heading: Who, Which, What
sections.rule: Who = persons (indefinite). Which = one out of a group. What = things or profession. Who is he? = name. What is he? = profession. Which is he? = point out from a group.
sections.bn: Who = ব্যক্তি। Which = দলের মধ্যে কে/কোনটি। What = বস্তু বা পেশা।
examples: Who are you?
What is he? — He is a doctor.
Which of these do you want?

sections.heading: Each, Either, Neither
sections.rule: Each, either, neither separate one from a group. Either/neither refer to two. Each can refer to any number. They take singular verbs and singular pronouns.
sections.bn: Each, either, neither দল থেকে একজনকে আলাদা করে। Either/neither = দুইজনের মধ্যে। এরা singular verb নেয়।
examples: Either will do.
Each of the girls has done her work.

sections.heading: Reflexive vs Emphatic
sections.rule: Same form (-self / -selves). Reflexive: the doer is both subject and object (I hurt myself). Emphatic: used for emphasis (I myself saw him). Emphatic pronouns cannot stand alone as subject.
sections.bn: একই রূপ। Reflexive = কর্তা নিজেই কর্ম। Emphatic = জোর দেওয়ার জন্য। Emphatic একা subject হতে পারে না।
examples: I hurt myself. (Reflexive)
I myself saw the man. (Emphatic)

sections.heading: Any, Some, One, None, Others, They
sections.rule: Indefinite pronouns refer to persons/things in a general way. One must be followed by one/one's (not he/his). None can be singular or plural. They can mean people in general.
sections.bn: Indefinite Pronoun সাধারণভাবে ব্যক্তি/বস্তু বোঝায়। One-এর সাথে one/one's ব্যবহার করুন।
examples: One must do one's duty.
They say a war will break out.

sections.heading: Each other / One another
sections.rule: Traditionally each other is used for two, one another for more than two. Modern usage often ignores the distinction.
sections.bn: সাধারণত each other = দুইজন; one another = দুইয়ের বেশি।
examples: Dutt and Sharma struck each other.
The boys fought with one another.

sections.heading: Chapter XII Preview
sections.rule: Verbs are of two main classes: Principal Verbs (used independently — call, go, work) and Auxiliary Verbs (help another verb to form voice, mood, tense — be, have, shall, will, may, do, can).
sections.bn: Verb দুই প্রকার: Principal Verb (নিজে কাজ করে) এবং Auxiliary Verb (অন্য verb-কে সাহায্য করে)।
examples: Principal: She works hard.
Auxiliary: She is working.
